entry: Action-adventure stealth video game for the [[PlayStation]], released in 1998 by Konami. [[Hideo Kojima]] directed, produced, and wrote the game, the third mainline installment in the [[Metal Gear]] series. Solid Snake, a former Special Forces operative, is pulled out of retirement to infiltrate Shadow Moses, a nuclear weapons facility seized by the rogue FOXHOUND unit. Critics praised its cinematic presentation, narrative, gameplay, and stealth mechanics, and it sold more than seven million copies worldwide. A remake, *Metal Gear Solid: The Twin Snakes*, appeared on the [[GameCube]] in 2004.

Japanese franchise of action-adventure stealth games created by [[Hideo Kojima]]. Konami developed and published the first game, Metal Gear, released in 1987 for MSX home computers. Players control a special forces operative, usually Solid Snake, who is assigned to find the titular superweapon, Metal Gear, a bipedal walking tank capable of launching nuclear weapons. The series is credited with pioneering and popularizing stealth games and cinematic video games. The franchise has sold 66.4 million units as of June 2026. [[Metal Gear Solid (video game)|Metal Gear Solid]] (1998) marked the series' move to 3D graphics and brought it international fame.

Type of [[Chemical bond|chemical bond]] in metals, arising from electrostatic attraction between delocalized conduction electrons and positively charged metal ions. Metal atoms lose their valence electrons to a large, delocalized electron cloud, leaving [[Ion|cations]] that form a crystal lattice held together by the negative charge of that cloud. It can be described as a more delocalized version of [[Covalent bond|covalent bonding]]. Metallic bonding accounts for many properties of metals, including strength, ductility, thermal and electrical conductivity, opacity, and luster. A metal can also show other bonds: elemental [[Gallium|gallium]] consists of covalently bound atom pairs that form a crystal structure with metallic bonding between them. Quantum mechanics later gave the picture a formal basis in the free electron model, which treats electrons as a gas moving through the solid.

Electrically conducting phase of hydrogen. Eugene Wigner and Hillard Bell Huntington predicted it in 1935 on theoretical grounds. At high pressure and temperature, metallic hydrogen can exist as a partial liquid rather than a solid. It is thought to occur in large quantities in the interiors of [[Jupiter]] and [[Saturn]], and in some [[Exoplanet|exoplanets]]. In 1968, Neil Ashcroft suggested that it might be a [[Superconductivity|superconductor]] up to room temperature (290 K or 17 °C). The initial pressure estimate of about 25 GPa was later shown to be too low; modern calculations point to around 400 GPa.

American heavy metal band formed in Los Angeles in 1981. Founding members James Hetfield and Lars Ulrich are the primary songwriters, and the band has been based in [[San Francisco]] for most of its career. Its fast tempos and aggressive musicianship helped make it one of the founding big four bands of thrash metal, with [[Megadeth]], Anthrax, and [[Slayer]]. Its 1986 album *Master of Puppets* brought commercial success, and the self-titled album of 1991 sold more than 16 million copies in the United States. Metallica led a 2000 lawsuit against [[Napster]] over copyrighted material and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2009. It has won ten [[Grammy Awards]] from 26 nominations and has sold more than 163 million albums worldwide as of 2023.

Relative abundance of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium in a [[Star|star]] or other astronomical object. Astronomers use the word metals for all elements except hydrogen and helium, a usage distinct from the chemical definition of a metal. Metallicity is most often expressed as [Fe/H], the logarithmic ratio of iron to hydrogen relative to the [[Sun]]'s value. Iron became the default reference element in the mid-20th century because it could be measured reliably. Heavy elements form in the cores of stars and are spread by stellar winds and [[Supernova|supernovae]]. Older stars formed in the metal-poor early universe and generally have lower metallicities than younger stars. In exoplanet systems, stars with elevated metallicity are more likely to host giant [[Planet|planets]].

Element, or category of elements, with properties intermediate between metals and nonmetals. The word comes from the Latin *metallum*, meaning metal, but there is no standard definition of a metalloid and no complete agreement on which elements qualify. The six commonly recognized metalloids are [[Boron]], [[Silicon]], [[Germanium]], [[Arsenic]], [[Antimony]], and [[Tellurium]]. Carbon, aluminum, selenium, polonium, and astatine are less frequently classified as metalloids. Typical metalloids look metallic, may be brittle, and are only fair conductors of electricity. They and their compounds are used in alloys, catalysts, flame retardants, glasses, [[Semiconductor|semiconductors]], and electronics. Metalloids are sometimes called semimetals, a practice that has been discouraged because semimetal more commonly denotes a specific kind of electronic band structure.

Process of shaping and reshaping metals to create useful objects, parts, and large structures. Modern metalworking falls into three broad areas: forming, cutting, and joining. Its roots predate recorded history, when people worked soft native metals such as [[Gold|gold]] with simple hand tools. The oldest archaeological evidence of copper working is a pendant from [[Iraq|northern Iraq]] dated to 8,700 BCE. Later came [[Smelting|smelting]] of ores and hot forging of [[Iron|iron]], and modern techniques include machining and [[Welding|welding]]. Metalworking has been an industry, a driver of [[Trade|trade]], a hobby, and an art. Machine shops hold a wide range of machine tools for precise products, while blacksmithing is no longer economically competitive on a large scale in developed countries.

Engineered material with properties arising from its designed structure rather than its chemical makeup. Metamaterials are typically fashioned from metals and plastics arranged in repeating patterns smaller than the [[Wavelength|wavelengths]] of the waves they affect. Their shape, geometry, size, and arrangement let them block, absorb, enhance, or bend electromagnetic, acoustic, or seismic waves. Those with a negative [[Refractive index|refractive index]] for particular wavelengths have drawn much research. Potential applications include [[Sports equipment|sports equipment]], optical filters, medical devices, sensor systems, and lenses for high-gain [[Antenna (radio)|antennas]]. Researchers have also demonstrated a form of invisibility using gradient-index materials. Metamaterial research is interdisciplinary, drawing on electrical engineering, [[Optics|optics]], solid-state physics, and nanoscience.

Rock altered by heat, pressure, or chemically active fluids without fully melting. Metamorphic rock forms from a parent rock called the protolith, which may be igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic. Temperatures greater than 150 to 200 °C (300 to 400 °F) and elevated pressure of 100 megapascals (1,000 bar) or more cause the rock to recrystallize while it remains mostly solid. Metamorphic rocks make up a large part of the [[Earth's crust]] and form 12% of Earth's land surface. Common examples include [[Gneiss]], [[Slate]], [[Marble]], [[Schist]], and quartzite. Studying them reveals the temperatures and pressures that occur at great depths within the crust. The importance of heat was first noted by [[James Hutton]], who is often described as the father of modern geology.

Latin narrative poem by [[Ovid]] in dactylic hexameter. Composed around 8 CE, *Metamorphoses* contains 15 books and over 250 myths, tracing the history of the world from its creation to the deification of [[Julius Caesar]]. The poem defies simple genre classification, though it is generally considered to meet the criteria for an epic. Ovid drew on earlier metamorphosis poetry but diverged significantly from his models, and the work is organized around thematic transformation rather than linear chronology. It inspired [[Dante Alighieri|Dante]], [[Giovanni Boccaccio]], [[Geoffrey Chaucer]], and [[William Shakespeare]], and many of its episodes appeared in sculpture, painting, and music, especially during the [[Renaissance]]. The first of many English translations, by William Caxton, appeared in 1480.

Conspicuous, relatively abrupt change in an animal's body structure during its development. Some [[Insect|insects]], fish, amphibians, mollusks, crustaceans, cnidarians, echinoderms, and tunicates undergo metamorphosis, often with a change in nutrition or behavior. Animals with complete metamorphosis pass through radically different stages, while those with incomplete metamorphosis change between somewhat similar stages. In insects, [[Hormone|hormones]] control the process: ecdysone induces molting, and juvenile hormone prevents adult features during molts. Holometabolous insects enter an inactive [[Pupa|pupal]] stage, called a chrysalis in butterflies, before emerging as adults. Amphibians such as [[Frog|frogs]] transform from [[Tadpole|tadpoles]] into terrestrial adults. The evolution of metamorphosis in insects is thought to have fueled their dramatic radiation.

Collection of texts by [[Aristotle]] on substance, causation, and first philosophy. Many of Aristotle's works are highly compressed, and the treatises are often thought to be lecture notes. The title, from the Greek for those after the physics, reflects the work's place after the *Physics* in an arrangement by Andronicus of Rhodes. The text covers substance theory, different kinds of causation, form and matter, and the existence of mathematical objects. Book Alpha surveys earlier philosophers' views on first principles and causes, from the Ionian monists up to [[Plato]]. Book Lambda culminates in an eternal, unmoved mover that serves as the final cause of cosmic motion. The order in which the books were written is unknown, since later editors arranged them.

Spread of a pathogenic agent from a primary site to a secondary site in the body. The term usually refers to a cancerous tumor, and the new sites are called metastases. Cancer cells can penetrate blood or lymphatic vessels and travel to other tissues, where they form a secondary tumor resembling the original. [[Breast cancer]] that spreads to the lungs forms a tumor called metastatic breast cancer, not lung cancer. In the TNM staging system, metastasis is represented by the letter M and places a cancer in Stage IV. The chance of curative treatment is greatly reduced once a cancer has metastasized.

Celestial event of meteors seemingly radiating from one point in the night sky, caused by streams of cosmic debris. Meteor showers occur when [[Meteoroid|meteoroids]] enter Earth's atmosphere at high speed on parallel trajectories. Most meteors are smaller than a grain of sand and disintegrate before reaching the ground. The Meteor Data Centre lists over 900 suspected showers, about 100 of them well established. Very intense showers are called meteor storms, producing at least 1,000 meteors an hour, most notably the Leonids. In 1794, Ernst Chladni proposed that meteors originated in [[Outer space|outer space]]. In 1866, Giovanni Schiaparelli showed that the Leonids shared an orbit with Comet Tempel, linking meteor showers to [[Comet|comets]].

Rock from outer space, fallen to the surface of a planet or moon. Meteorites are traditionally divided into stony meteorites, mainly of silicate minerals; iron meteorites, largely of ferronickel; and stony-iron meteorites, which contain both metallic and rocky material. Meteorites recovered after being observed during their fall are called falls, and all others are finds. Most originate from a handful of asteroid breakup events in the [[Asteroid belt|asteroid belt]]. Iron meteoroids transit the atmosphere most easily and cause most of the hypervelocity impact craters on Earth. The [[Tunguska event]] probably resulted from a stony or icy body that disintegrated in the atmosphere without leaving a crater. Meteorites have also been found on the [[Moon]] and [[Mars]].

Small body in outer space, ranging from grains up to one meter wide and far smaller than an asteroid. Most meteoroids come from the [[Asteroid belt|asteroid belt]], perturbed by planetary gravity, while others are particles from [[Comet|comets]] that give rise to [[Meteor shower|meteor showers]]. Some are impact debris ejected from the [[Moon]] or [[Mars]]. An estimated 25 million meteoroids, micrometeoroids, and other space debris enter Earth's atmosphere each day, which results in an estimated 15,000 metric tons (16,535 short tons) entering each year. Stony meteoroids that contain grain-like inclusions are called chondrites. In 2017 the International Astronomical Union revised the definition to objects between 30 μm and one meter in diameter.

Scientific study of the Earth's atmosphere and short-term weather, focusing on forecasting. Its applications include the military, aviation, energy production, transport, agriculture, construction, and disaster management. Together with [[Climatology|climatology]], atmospheric physics, and atmospheric chemistry, it forms the broader atmospheric sciences. Meteorologists use instruments such as thermometers, barometers, weather satellites, balloons, buoys, and radars to forecast weather at local, regional, and global scales. Ancient civilizations relied on folklore and astrology, and [[Aristotle]]'s treatise *Meteorology* summarized early observations. Numerical weather prediction in the 20th century, coupled with computers, transformed forecasting. Because the atmosphere is chaotic, uncertainty remains, a limit described by the [[Butterfly effect|butterfly effect]].

First-line oral medication for type 2 diabetes, sold as Glucophage among other brands. It works by decreasing glucose production in the [[Liver|liver]] and increasing the [[Insulin|insulin]] sensitivity of body tissues. It has a small risk of causing [[Hypoglycemia|low blood sugar]], and it is not associated with weight gain. Common adverse effects include [[Diarrhea|diarrhea]], nausea, and abdominal pain. It is also used for [[Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome|polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome]]. It was first described in 1922, introduced in France in 1957, and is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines.

Potent synthetic [[Opioid|opioid]] used to treat chronic pain and opioid use disorder. Taken daily, it relieves cravings and opioid withdrawal symptoms. Withdrawal management can take less than a month, or the drug may be maintained for life. Serious risks include respiratory depression and abnormal heart rhythms caused by a prolonged QT interval. It was developed in Germany in the late 1930s and approved in the [[United States]] in 1947 as an analgesic. It has been used in addiction treatment since the 1960s.

[[Central nervous system]] stimulant used mainly as a recreational or performance-enhancing drug. It is less commonly prescribed as a second-line treatment for [[Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder|attention deficit hyperactivity disorder]]. It has also been researched as a potential treatment for [[Brain injury|traumatic brain injury]]. It was discovered in 1893 and exists as two enantiomers, of which the dextro form is more potent. Overdose or extended binges may cause [[Psychosis|psychosis]], seizures, and bleeding in the brain. Methamphetamine has a high abuse liability, and discontinuing heavy use can lead to a post-acute-withdrawal syndrome that can persist for months.

Simplest [[Alkane|alkane]] hydrocarbon, CH₄, and the main constituent of [[Natural gas]]. Methane is an odorless, colorless gas at standard temperature and pressure, with one carbon atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms in a tetrahedral shape. It boils at −161.5 °C at one atmosphere and is flammable at concentrations of 5.4% to 17% in air. Methane is transparent to visible light but absorbs infrared radiation, which makes it a [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gas]]. Its largest reservoir is beneath the seafloor as methane clathrates. Its primary reactions are [[Combustion]], steam reforming to [[Syngas]], and halogenation, and methane has been detected on [[Mars]]. Its heat of combustion is 55.5 MJ/kg.

Simplest [[Alcohol (chemistry)|aliphatic alcohol]], CH₃OH, also called methyl alcohol or wood alcohol. It is a light, volatile, colorless, and flammable liquid with an odor similar to ethanol, but it is more acutely toxic. Methanol was once made by the destructive distillation of wood, but it is now mainly produced by hydrogenating [[Carbon monoxide]]. More than 20 million tons are produced annually as a precursor to [[Formaldehyde]], [[Acetic acid|acetic acid]], and other commodity chemicals. [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptians]] used a mixture containing methanol in embalming, and [[Robert Boyle]] first isolated it in 1661 by distilling boxwood. Methanol is also abundant in star-forming regions of space, where astronomers use it as a marker.

Protestant Christian tradition derived from the life and teachings of [[John Wesley]]. Methodism began as a revival movement within the [[Church of England]] in the 18th century and became a separate denomination after Wesley's death. Wesleyan theology emphasizes sanctification and the transforming effect of the [[Holy Spirit]] on Christian character. Unlike Calvinist doctrine, it holds that salvation is achievable for all, and it rejects [[Predestination|predestination]]. Worship ranges from high to low church, and Methodism is known for its rich musical tradition of [[Hymn|hymns]], much of it written by Charles Wesley. Methodists are also known for charity, including hospitals, orphanages, soup kitchens, and schools. Most Methodist denominations belong to the World Methodist Council, and the movement has about 50 million adherents worldwide.

Study of research methods, and the philosophical assumptions behind them. A method is a structured procedure for reaching a goal, such as acquiring knowledge or verifying knowledge claims. Methodologies are traditionally divided into [[Quantitative research|quantitative]] and [[Qualitative research|qualitative]] research. Quantitative research is the main methodology of the natural sciences, using precise numerical measurements to find universal laws. The dominant approach there is the [[Scientific method]], which includes observation, formulating a [[Hypothesis|hypothesis]], testing it by experiment, and publishing the findings. Qualitative research, more characteristic of the [[Social science|social sciences]], seeks an in-depth understanding of meaning and relies on methods such as surveys and interviews. In recent decades, many social scientists have adopted mixed-methods research, which combines both approaches. A few theorists reject methodology as a discipline, while methodologists argue that a good methodology helps researchers reach reliable theories efficiently.
